The city above was built on bedrock, but Arthur’s workshop was built on silence.

It sat three levels below the subway line, past abandoned pneumatic tube stations and rusted water mains from the turn of the nineteenth century. Here, the air smelled perpetually of ozone, old wool, and damp limestone. Arthur was seventy-two, or perhaps seventy-four—he had stopped keeping track when his hair turned from silver slate to chalky white. His title, inscribed on a brass plate beside his oak desk, read *Curator of Unclaimed Echoes*.

Every day, thousands of memories slipped silently out of human minds. Most vanished entirely, dissolving like salt in warm broth. But some were too dense to dissolve. They were the half-remembered melodies from forgotten summers, the names of childhood pets, the shade of yellow on an ex-lover’s raincoat, or the exact scent of rain striking dry soil on an August afternoon thirty years ago. When a memory was abandoned—dropped through the frayed pockets of routine—it drifted downward through the earth.

It was Arthur’s job to catch them before they fell into the dark waters of the subterranean sump.

He worked with silver tweezers and an array of clear glass vials. When an echo fell through the copper funnel in his ceiling, it sounded like a dry leaf striking glass. He would catch it mid-air, hold it up to his brass desk lamp, and examine its hue.

A pale blue vapor signified regret. A spark of copper-red indicated sudden, unexpressed affection. A velvety navy blue was a vivid dream forgotten upon waking.

Today had been slow. By four in the afternoon, Arthur had cataloged nine distinct echoes:

1. A telephone number from 1988 belonging to a girl named Clara, who had moved to Seattle.
2. The taste of a specific brand of cinnamon candy discontinued in 1974.
3. The feeling of swimming at dusk in a quarry when the water was warmer than the air.
4. A stray dog’s pattern of spots, remembered by an accountant in Chicago.
5. The third verse of a lullaby sung by a grandmother whose grand-daughter now spoke only French.
6. The weight of a wooden marble held inside a pocket during a spelling bee.
7. A quiet promise made under a streetlight that neither party had intended to break, yet both failed to keep.
8. The smell of cedar chips sitting in an attic on a Tuesday in October.
9. The physical sensation of turning sixteen while sitting on a cold porch railing.

Arthur sealed the wooden marble memory into a glass phial, corked it, dipped the neck in black beeswax, and wrote the coordinates on a tag: *Shelf 402, Row B, Item 11,894.*

The shelves stretched into the gloom for half a mile. Millions of tiny bottles glowing with faint hues illuminated the stone walls like fireflies. No one ever came to retrieve them. In forty years, Arthur had only received one visitor—a woman in a yellow coat who had lost the memory of her mother’s voice. She wept when he found it, held the bottle to her ear, and left without saying goodbye. He hadn't minded. The work was not meant for gratitude; it was meant for preservation.

At five o'clock, as Arthur prepared his evening tea, the copper funnel hummed.

It was a strange noise—a deep, bell-like chime that vibrated through the floorboards.

Arthur set his kettle down and hurried to the desk.

An echo was floating down the chute, but it wasn't vapor or a spark. It was a solid orb, the size of a plum, radiating a warm, golden amber light that smelled faintly of honeysuckle and old books. It landed in the velvet tray with a soft thud.

Arthur picked up his magnifying loupe and leaned close. Inside the amber sphere, images shifted rapidly, like film on fast-forward.

He saw a garden behind a red-brick cottage. He saw a wooden table with two teacups. He saw a woman with laugh lines around her eyes, turning to look warmly at someone off-camera. He saw a pair of hands—his own hands, younger, unspotted by age—reaching out to touch her cheek. He heard a soft laugh echo through the brass cone above.

Arthur froze. His heart gave a painful lurch against his ribs.

It was a memory of his own.

He had forgotten her. He didn't even remember forgetting her. The memory had slipped away long ago, buried under decades of organizing discarded moments, until he believed he had always been alone in this dark room.

He stared at the golden sphere. The light pulsed in time with his breathing.

If he uncorked the bottle, he could breathe the memory back. He would remember her name. He would remember her voice, the taste of her tea, and the reason he had left the surface world to sit among these damp stones.

He reached out with two fingers. His hands, usually steady, were trembling.

"Why did I let you go?" he whispered to the glass.

The amber light flickered, warm and silent. It offered no answers, only the weight of having once been deeply loved on a sunny afternoon in a garden that no longer existed.

He picked up a small silver hammer used for sealing wax. One light tap would break the glass.

Arthur raised the hammer. He held it suspended in the dim air. Above him, through yards of rock, he heard a subway train—hundreds of people rushing home to dinners they would forget and faces that would blur.

Slowly, Arthur lowered the hammer.

Using his tweezers, he lifted the golden orb. He did not break it. He placed it inside a crystal cylinder, poured hot red wax over the cork, and waited for it to cool.

He picked up his pen and wrote on the tag:

*Item 000,001. An afternoon in June. Loved, remembered, and left unbroken.*

He walked to the end of the longest aisle, where light barely reached. There was an empty spot on the top shelf, reserved since his first day. He set his memory upon the wooden ledge.

The amber light glowed softly, casting a warm halo across the stone wall.

Arthur turned off his lamp, sat in his wooden rocking chair, and poured his tea. Outside, the quiet river of forgotten moments flowed past, but in the dark, he closed his eyes, knowing that somewhere on the shelf behind him, he was still young, and the sun was still shining on the garden.
